nodes.label: Q24: Migrating a monolith to microservices
Strangler fig pattern
nodes.rationale: A facade in front of the monolith lets one capability at a time be routed to a new service. Preferred over a big-bang rewrite, which means chasing a moving target with two systems to maintain. There is no prize for eliminating the monolith — stop when it stops paying.

nodes.label: Most of the work is untangling, not extraction
nodes.rationale: In the monolith, escalating a risk raises an issue, drops project health and flags the benefit — three services' worth of work in one method and one transaction. Someone has to find that method and every one like it and turn it into a message.

nodes.label: Split the data first, logically
nodes.rationale: The skipped step that stalls migrations: stop the rest of the monolith joining to a module's tables and force access through an interface. If you cannot do that inside one process you certainly cannot do it across a network.

nodes.label: Modular monolith as the honest halfway house
nodes.rationale: Sometimes the right place to stop. Stalling halfway is not automatically a failure — a monolith plus three well-chosen services is a fine architecture; the failure mode is stalling with a shared database, which is strictly worse than where you started.

nodes.label: Extraction order — Reporting first
nodes.rationale: Reporting is read-only with no writes to move and no consistency risk, so it proves the outbox, broker, pipeline and monitoring before anything that writes moves; then Benefits, KPI, the hard Risk/Issues pair, and Projects last because it is the hub. The goal of the first extraction is learning the mechanics, not delivering value.

nodes.label: What the migration adds that never existed
nodes.rationale: Outbox in every publisher, inbox in every consumer, compensation for every distributed operation, correlation ids and tracing, a read model plus rebuild, contract versioning, and per-service pipelines, dashboards and on-call. That list is the cost of the migration; anyone who cannot name it has not done one.
